item.description: Federal Statistical Office: 79,121 border guards in the Canton of Ticino in Q2 2026, up 505 units (+0.64%) compared to Q1. Quarterly BFS data analysis.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell
- 79,121 border crossers in Ticino in Q2 2026, up quarterly - +0.64% vs Q1 2026 (+505 units); -0.57% on an annual basis - Distribution: 61.6% men, 38.4% women - Average age: 78% are between 30 and 59 years old
## Key facts
- **Number**: 79,121 border guards - When: 2026-Q2 (official BFS data) - Where: Canton Ticino, Switzerland - Who: Federal Statistical Office (BFS) - QoQ change: +505 units (+0.64%) vs Q1 - YoY variation: -457 units (-0.57%) vs Q2 2025 - Gender: Men 61.6%, Women 38.4%
The Federal Statistical Office (BFS) announced the number of border workers in the Canton of Ticino at the end of the second quarter of 2026: 79,121 people, up compared to the previous three months. The quarter therefore qualifies as an increase: the cyclical variation compared to Q1 2026 is positive by 505 units, equal to +0.64%. On an annual basis, however, the comparison with Q2 2025 shows a slight drop of 457 units (-0.57%), a sign of some volatility in the composition of the Ticino cross-border workforce.
### Quarterly change: the rebound from Q1
In the first quarter of 2026, the BFS statistic had recorded 78,616 border crossers. The recovery of 505 units in the following quarter represents a sign of stabilization after the winter months, when traditionally the number of members of the Federal Register of border workers tends to contract. The +0.64% growth, albeit modest, signals a positive trend in the labour market ### Reading the historical series: seasonal volatility and underlying trend
Looking at the eight quarters available from the BFS, the curve of the Ticino border crossers describes a trend that isfar from linear. In the first quarter of relevance (Q3 2024), the number reached 79,808, representing the maximum peak of the period examined. From there, the flow entered a phase of slight decline, reaching an all-time low in Q4 2025 with 78,698 border crossers. In the following quarter (Q1 2026), the contraction continued to 78,616, marking the point of greatest relative weakness. In Q2 2026 alone, the number rose to 79,121, while still remaining far from the 2024 high.
This trajectory suggests two fundamental considerations. First, seasonal volatility continues to weigh, with winter quarters (Q4, Q1) historically showing a contraction of a few hundred units. Second: net of seasonality, the underlying trend is oscillation around a range of 78,600-79,600 border crossers, without a clear upward or downward direction on multi-year scales. The BFS data therefore indicate an apparent stability, but with underlying dynamics of constant turnover.
### Master composition: the centre of gravity between the ages of 30 and 59
The distribution by age classes provides an even more detailed picture of the Ticino border basin. The Q2 2026 quarter detects a strong concentration in the central productive age groups:
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Implications for Payslip and Job Stability
For those who work or intend to look for a job beyond the Ticino border, the FSO figure of 79,121 cross-border workers is, first and foremost, a mirror of the health of the labour market. A stable number, despite slight quarterly fluctuations, signals that the use of cross-border labour remains a consolidated practice in the Ticino economic fabric. This allows those already working in Ticino to maintain reasonable job security, while for those seeking work the employment pool remains considered appealing. You can simulate the impact of a Ticino contract on your net salary using the [salary calculator](nav:calculator), which takes into account rates consistent with the cross-border market.
At the same time, the figures suggest that competition has not decreased. With the annual decline of -0.57% (457 fewer units compared to Q2 2025), it is possible that some positions previously held by cross-border workers have been reassigned to Swiss residents or citizens of other nationalities, especially in sectors where qualification is high (IT, finance, specialist healthcare). Those working in Ticino as cross-border workers must therefore pay attention to their positioning in the market: a career crystallised in a low-qualification position could prove fragile, while the push towards skills updating (languages, professional certifications, digital skills) remains strategic.
### Pension Planning: OASI, LPP and LAMal
The 79,121 cross-border workers registered in Q2 2026 are equally contributors to the Swiss social security systems. Every person working in Switzerland is obliged to pay contributions to the Old Age and Survivors' Insurance (OASI), to the occupational pension system (LPP) and to health insurance (LAMal). For cross-border workers, it is essential to understand how these payments integrate with tax and contribution obligations in Italy, thus avoiding pension gaps at retirement.
The FSO data do not provide a breakdown by sector or average income level, but the prevalence of cross-border workers in the 50-54 age bracket (almost 11,000 people) underlines the importance of adequately planning retirement. When a cross-border worker reaches 65 in Switzerland, they will have accumulated years of OASI and LPP contributions that will affect the pension. Timely communication with INPS, the Italian body, and monitoring of LPP plans with the Swiss employer remain crucial. For higher incomes, it is also advisable to check whether payments into the third pillar (Pillar 3a) and cantonal tax rebates are structured optimally to maximise supplementary pension provision.
### Concrete Actions: How to Move Now
1. Check your contract and contributions: Ensure that the Swiss employer correctly pays OASI and LPP contributions. Request a statement of contributions from the local OASI Compensation Office, to make sure there are no gaps.
2. **Update your professional profile**: With a slightly negative annual trend, job stability is not guaranteed. Invest in refresher courses and keep your CV competitive by browsing [job listings](nav:jobs) in growing sectors (specialist healthcare, green energy, fintech).
3. Plan your cross-border taxation: The FSO data do not break down by average income, but you know that your Swiss income is subject to withholding tax in Ticino and to declaration in Italy. Use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) at least once a year to check the tax and pension impact on your payslip.
4. Monitor upcoming FSO data: The Federal Statistical Office publishes quarterly data regularly. If the next quarter signals a contraction greater than -1%, it will be time to reassess your contractual position or diversify your professional profile.
5. Consult a cross-border tax expert: For incomes exceeding CHF 150,000 per year, it is advisable to check whether deferral forms (second pillar, Pillar 3a, cantonal tax rebates) are structured correctly according to recent agreements between Switzerland and Italy.
Start today: access the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate your net income considering the gender composition data (61.6% men, 38.4% women) and by age bracket emerging from this FSO statistic. This will allow you to plan your pension and tax payments with awareness of the real employment trends in Ticino.

## In a nutshell - Unified AVS reference age at 65 years from 2024 - New Frontier Agreement in force from 1 January 2024 - Old frontier workers: exemption €7,500 until 2033 - New frontier workers: €10,000 exemption on tax at source
## Key facts - **What**: AVS pension advance possible up to 2 years before the reference age - When: AVS 21 reform in force since 2024, reference age 65 years - Where: Canton Ticino, for frontier workers with G permit - Who: AVS (Swiss first pillar), LPP (second pillar), INPS (Italy) - How it works: Withholding tax withheld only in Switzerland; Italy applies tax credit - Exemption for old frontier workers: €7,500, transitional regime 2024-2033 - New frontier tax exemption: €10,000 on tax at source - Regulatory reference: New Agreement signed on 23 December 2020, ratified by Law 83/2023
The reference age for the AVS annuity is set at 65 years for men and women from 2024, following the AVS 21 reform. Those who wish to advance their pension can do so up to two years beforehand, accepting a permanent reduction in their pension. For a border worker with family and children, the decision to anticipate retirement has direct effects on the second LPP pillar and coordination with the Italian INPS.
The AVS 21 reform also introduced a flexibility mechanism: it is possible to postpone the annuity beyond 65 years, obtaining a supplement calculated per year of Anticipating the AVS pension at 63 or 64 years old means accepting a permanent reduction in the first pillar pension. The penalty is more pronounced the further one moves away from the reference age of 65, and is also reflected in the amount of the LPP annuity, which is calculated on the accumulated old age at the time of exit. For a family with children still dependent or in the process of university studies, the economic framework changes significantly: early retirement reduces gross income but free time to devote to the family.
### Scenario comparison: anticipate or postpone Considering the Italian personal income tax rates in force — 23% up to €28,000, 35% from €28,001 to €50,000, 43% over €50,000 — a frontier worker who anticipates retirement could be in a lower bracket, with theoretical tax savings. However, the prepaid annuity is lower by law, and the replacement income (Swiss AVS annuity) will be taxed at source in Switzerland with subsequent tax credit in Italy. A comparison between scenarios, even hypothetical, shows that postponing by one or two years can significantly increase the overall AVS plus LPP income, useful to cover family expenses in the long term.
Coordination between Swiss AVS and Italian INPS depends on the worker's contributory history. Those who have contributed in both countries can accumulate the insurance periods, while the amount of the benefit is calculated pro rata. For

Planning early retirement for a cross-border commuter with a family requires several concrete operational steps. The first step is to request an updated AVS and LPP statement, in order to know the available retirement savings and the projected pension benefit. The second step consists of simulating the tax impact of the early withdrawal, taking into account the allowance provided for by the New Agreement: €10,000 for new cross-border commuters, €7,500 for old cross-border commuters under the 2024-2033 transitional regime.
### Operational checklist for the family The preparation phase involves comparing alternative scenarios, with the support of dedicated tools. The planning must consider the Swiss contributions still to be paid — AVS/AI/IPG at 5.3% borne by the employee, AD/AC at 1.1% up to the cap of CHF 148,200, LPP between 7% and 18% by age bracket from age 25 — and their effect on the future pension. For health coverage, cross-border commuters holding a G permit retain the right to choose LAMal, with adult deductibles ranging from CHF 300 to CHF 2,500, to be assessed in relation to post-retirement income.
### Tools and next steps To navigate the variables involved, it is useful to consult your LPP statement and request a pension projection from the pension fund. The AVS pension application must be submitted to the competent Swiss institution, while coordination with INPS follows the procedures set out in the Italy-Switzerland double taxation convention of 9 December 1976.

Rail traffic on the line connecting Arbedo-Castione to Biasca went haywire in the early afternoon of today, Monday. This was reported by the SBB online portal, which reported the interruption of rail connections on the route. The reason for the blockade is "one accident per person", as stated in the note published by the Swiss Federal Railways.
The incident was recorded in the midday band and resulted in the suppression of trains between the two stations. SBB reported that disruptions to rail traffic are expected to continue in the hours following the report, without at the moment providing a precise forecast on the resumption of regular service. The midday service disruption coincided with a time slot where many workers are on lunch breaks or commuting, while others use the train to return to residential areas.
The SBB note does not specify whether substitute bus services have been provided on the route concerned. In the absence of a ferry bus service, those who had to travel between the two locations were faced with two concrete options: wait for the resumption of the train service, communicated as uncertain in the following hours, or fold back on their own vehicle or on alternative routes by road. The Gotthard motorway tunnel and the cantonal road represent the road routes parallel to the railway line, but offer very different timing and frequencies compared to the train.

item.title: Canicola in the construction sites: Unia asks for mandatory breaks
item.description: Only 18% receive systematic breaks above 33°C. Out of 984 workers interviewed, 82% of construction sites ignore the protections provided. This is what the union is asking for.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Eight out of ten construction sites do not apply the mandatory breaks above 33°C - Unia asks for suspension of heavy work at 33 degrees and effective sanctions - Survey of 984 construction workers: only 18% have systematic time breaks - Ticino indicated as an example: suspension of work from 14:00 in heat waves
## Key facts - **What**: Unia survey on compliance with anti-heat measures in Swiss construction sites - When: July (interviews); results presented in Bern - Where: Switzerland (with positive mention of the Canton of Ticino) - Who: Unia trade union, 984 construction workers interviewed, Suva cited as technical source - Amount/Share: 18% with systematic breaks; 67% never; 15% sometimes; 32% with systematic cool place; 43% occasional; 25% without; 68% without early hours; 15% ill; +7% accident risk above 30°C - Proposal: Maximum threshold 33°C in the building works ordinance; breaks of 15 min/hour counted as work
In July, the Unia union interviewed 984 construction workers in all regions of Switzerland to verify the application of heat protection measures on construction sites. The results, presented in Bern, paint a critical picture: only 18% of respondents systematically benefit from 15-minute breaks per hour starting at 33 degrees. 67% state that such breaks are never granted, while 15% receive them "sometimes".
Even resting places remain a problem. Only a third (32%) of workers The Unia survey opens a trade union front that will also weigh in on Canton Ticino, where the construction sector permanently employs a significant share of Italian border workers. The data speak of a leopard-spot application of the protections already provided by law: 82% of Swiss shipyards do not regularly grant anti-heat breaks above 33°C and 25% of workers do not even have a cool place to stop.
For border crossers who cross the Brogeda, Chiasso or Gaggiolo crossings every morning towards the Lugano, Mendrisiotto or Bellinzonese shipyards, the question is not theoretical. Working at 14:00 with 35-39°C exposes you to an accident risk that, according to Suva data cited by Unia, grows by 7% above 30°C. 15% of respondents report personal or colleague illnesses: a share that, on an average site of ten workers, statistically corresponds to one or two episodes per season.
### What Unia is asking for and what it would actually change The union makes three precise requests. The first is the inclusion in the building works ordinance of a maximum threshold of 33°C: beyond this temperature, heavy outdoor physical work should be stopped, except for guaranteeing 15-minute breaks every hour in an air-conditioned place, counted as paid working hours.
The second request concerns controls: Unia asks Suva to strengthen inspections and, in case of incapacity, to entrust the task to the Cantons or
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). For a Ticino cross-border worker employed on a construction site, the first concrete step is to document. In the absence of a mandatory register of interruptions, it is advisable to keep a personal diary of the breaks granted or denied, the hours actually worked and the temperatures perceived. These notes become useful evidence in the event of illness, a wage dispute or a claim for compensation.
### Procedure in the event of illness on the construction site If a worker suffers heat-related illness, the chain of actions to follow is clear. First: immediately notify the site supervisor and, if the situation allows it, contact the emergency number. Second: be accompanied to a cool and shaded place, drink water, and stop all physical effort. Third: even if the illness seems to have passed, report it to your trusted doctor and keep any certificates, which are useful for any mandatory insurance coverage (UVG/LAA, KV/HIA for those who have opted for the Swiss system, daily allowance in the event of inability to work).
### Practical steps to enforce your rights Construction workers can contact the Unia union offices in Ticino for assistance on breaks not granted, unsuitable hours or the absence of rest areas. Reports can also be sent to Suva, which is responsible for occupational safety, and to SECO for matters relating to employment conditions. In the event of forced interruptions linked to bad weather, the existing compensation system does not currently cover heatwaves: the Unia proposal to extend compensation to heat is still awaiting passage in the Council of States.
### Useful tools on the portal To find your way around the economic and contribution aspects linked to a possible suspension of the construction site — salary, AVS/LPP contributions, allowances — it is useful to consult the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to estimate actual pay in the event of forced breaks. For those considering a change of sector or wanting to compare the conditions offered, the [job offers](nav:jobs) section collects open positions in Ticino.
Unia's pressure is not only union-based: if the 33°C threshold becomes mandatory, cross-border workers will also be able to count on written protection, no longer left to the discretion of the individual site supervisor.

## Key facts - **What**: Italian-Swiss social security agreement distinct from the tax convention - When: New Agreement from 1 January 2024; transitional regime 2024–2033 - Where: Canton of Ticino and border Italy (Chiasso, Brogeda, Gaggiolo crossings) - Who: AFC/ESTV (tax at source), INPS, Revenue Agency - Amount: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3%; AD 1.1% up to CHF 148,200; LPP 7–18% by age group - When signed: New Agreement 23 December 2020; Italian ratification Law 83 of 13 June 2023

item.title: Border tax credit 2026: common errors
item.description: Framework EC of 730, new Agreement in force since 2024 and transitional regime: the most frequent errors of border workers.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - New Frontier Agreement signed on 23/12/2020, in force from 1 January 2024 - Old frontier workers: exemption €7,500, transitional regime 2024–2033 - New frontier workers: deductible €10,000 - Withholding tax withheld only in Switzerland, credit in EC framework of 730
## Key facts - **What**: Tax credit to avoid double taxation on employee income in Switzerland - When: Income tax return 2026 (income 2025), second year of full operation of the new regime - Where: Canton of Ticino and the rest of Switzerland, declaration in Italy - Who: Frontier workers with G permit, INPS, Revenue Agency - Amount: Exemption €7,500 (old border guards), deductible €10,000 (new border guards) - Regulatory reference: Law 83 of 13/6/2023 (Italian ratification), Convention of 9 December 1976 - Declaratory framework: EC of model 730
The tax credit for border workers working in the Canton of Ticino — or more generally in Switzerland — is the mechanism by which Italy avoids double taxation on income produced overseas. From 1 January 2024, the new Agreement between Rome and Bern is in force, signed on 23 December 2020 and ratified by Italy with Law 83 of 13 June 2023. The 2026 tax return, relating to 2025 income, represents the second year of full operation of the updated regime.
### How credit works in the EC framework For frontier workers, the tax at source is withheld ## Practical analysis: where errors tend to concentrate
The experience of the last two filing campaigns — 2024 (for 2023 income, the launch year) and 2025 (for 2024 income, the first full year) — has brought to light a series of recurring critical issues. These are not data from a single study, but consolidated patterns that the Italian Revenue Agency and cross-border CAFs report in their operational communications.
### Mistake 1 — Confusing the tax credit with a refund Many taxpayers believe that Section CE generates a monetary credit from the Italian tax authority. In reality, the mechanism is different: the tax credit absorbs Italian IRPEF up to the amount of tax already paid in Switzerland. If the foreign tax exceeds the Italian one, the taxpayer does not receive anything extra; if the Italian tax is higher, they only pay the difference. Confusing this mechanism leads to entering incorrect amounts in the 730 form or to requesting unfounded refunds.
### Mistake 2 — Forgetting the Swiss payslip Swiss source deductions are not data that the Italian Revenue Agency receives automatically. They must be reported by the taxpayer based on the salary certificate issued by the Swiss employer. Omitting this entry — or entering an amount different from what was actually withheld — produces a tax credit inconsistent with the declared income, with possible anomaly flags.
### Mistake 3 — Failing to update the cross-border status Those who in 2025 switched from old to new cross-border status, or vice versa, must reconstruct the taxable base taking into account the different exemptions (€7,500 versus €10,000). The same applies to those who changed employer or canton: the source-tax rate varies, and Section CE must be populated with the correct data.
### Scenario comparison | Regime | Threshold/exemption | Declaration section | Error risk | |---|---|---|---| | Old cross-border (pre 17/7/2023) | €7,500 | CE with transitional period 2024–2033 | Medium | | New cross-border (post 17/7/2023) | €10,000 | Standard CE | High if the time cutoff is not known | | Commuter beyond 20 km | No special exemption | CE + double taxation check | High |
The table is not exhaustive: every situation must be assessed with your own CAF or advisor, but it captures the three most common scenarios among Canton Ticino workers. For details on the calculation, the [tax calculator for cross-border workers](nav:calculator) is useful, as it simulates the gross Swiss tax and the Italian credit.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ## What to do concretely: the step-by-step procedure
### Step 1 — Gather the documentation Before opening the 730 form, the cross-border worker must obtain: Swiss salary certificate (Lohnausweis), monthly pay slips, statement of AHV/AI/IPG contributions (5.3% borne by the employee) and AD/AC (1.1% with a cap of CHF 148,200), any LPP contributions (7–18% by age bracket, from age 25) and LAINF (0.7–1.5%). Without these documents, section CE cannot be filled out correctly.
### Step 2 — Verify the cross-border worker category Old or new cross-border worker — the distinction makes a difference: €7,500 exemption versus €10,000 allowance. The data must be cross-checked with the start date of the employment relationship in Switzerland.
### Step 3 — Fill out section CE In row CE3, the gross Swiss income must be indicated; in the following row, the foreign tax withheld. The software will calculate the credit due. ⚠️ A frequent mistake is to enter the net Swiss income instead of the gross: the credit would be understated.
### Step 4 — Submit the return and keep the documents The ordinary deadline for the 730 is 30 September (pre-filled form) or end of November (with CAF). It is essential to keep the Lohnausweis for at least five years, in case of an audit.
### Operational checklist - Lohnausweis 2025 received from the employer - Pay slips reconciled with the annual gross - AHV, LPP, LAINF contributions verified - Old/new cross-border worker status confirmed - Section CE completed with gross income (not net) - Foreign tax corresponding to the Lohnausweis
### When a preventive simulation is worthwhile For those who changed regime in 2025 or have multiple Swiss employers, it is worth running a simulation with the [net salary calculator](nav:payslip) before submitting. This helps detect category and rate errors.
For taxpayers who wish to verify the impact of pension contributions — AHV, LPP and any third pillar 3a — the dedicated [pillar 3a](nav:pillar3) page is also available. On the insurance side, the [LAMal guide for cross-border workers](nav:health) clarifies the healthcare coverage options.
To avoid the most common pitfalls of section CE and obtain an up-to-date 2026 simulation, use the [salary calculator for cross-border workers](nav:calculator) before submitting the return.

item.title: 2026 tax credit: calculation for family with children
item.description: Frontier workers with children: CE framework of 730, deductible €10,000 new and €7,500 old. Calculation of tax credit, withholding tax withheld in Switzerland, return deadlines 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Box CE of 730: tax credit from Swiss withholdings CHF - 2026 exemption: €10,000 new cross-border workers, €7,500 old until 2033 - New Agreement effective January 1, 2024, avoids double taxation
## Key facts - **What**: Tax credit for recovery of source tax withheld only in Switzerland - When: 2026 tax return (year 2025); Agreement effective 1/1/2024 - Where: Box CE, Italian 730 form at the Revenue Agency - Who: Cross-border workers with Permit G (dependent work in Ticino/Switzerland) - Amount: €10,000 exemption for new, €7,500 exemption for old (transitional 2024-2033) - Source tax: Withheld ONLY in Switzerland (5.3% AVS/AI/IPG employee) - Bilateral convention: December 9, 1976 Italy-Switzerland (avoids double taxation)
In 2026, cross-border workers with children working in Ticino will continue to benefit from the tax credit for source taxes withheld in Switzerland. The system works as follows: Switzerland withholds income tax on work income according to its rates (AVS/AI/IPG 5.3% for employees, plus any insurance contributions LAINF 0.7–1.5% and cantonal); Italy, applying the bilateral convention of December 9, 1976 and the New Cross-border Agreement effective January 1, 2024, recognizes the tax credit in the 730 form, box CE, thus avoiding double taxation. The Italian return accounts for differentiated exemptions: €10,000 for cross-border workers who became such after July 17, 2023 (new), €7,500 for old cross-border workers with transitional regime until 2033.
The practical consequence is that, within the limits of the exemption, the amount paid in Switzerland is deducted from the Italian taxable income, reducing overall tax pressure. For families with children, the advantage increases thanks to family allowances and deductions for family dependents, which Italy recognizes in the return. Using the [salary and tax calculator](nav:calculator), you can simulate the impact of the exemption on your net income.
### How the New Agreement changed the framework The New Cross-border Agreement, signed December 23, 2020 and effective January 1, 2024 (ratified in Italy with Law 83 of June 13, 2023), introduced a clear differentiation between old and new cross-border workers. The old ones (already such before July 17, 2023) benefit from a €7,500 exemption in transitional regime until 2033; the new ones have a permanent €10,000 flat exemption. This means that the first euro of income beyond the exemption is subject to ordinary Italian tax according to IRPEF rates (23% up to €28,000, 35% up to €50,000, 43% above €50,000). Before January 2024, the mechanism was less defined; the Agreement has standardized and clarified the procedure, facilitating tax planning for families. In concrete terms, how does the calculation of the tax credit for a border family with children in 2026 work?
### Scenario: border crossing with two children A border worker with two children, employed in Ticino with annual gross income, suffers Swiss withholdings from Switzerland (5.3% for AVS/AI/IPG employee, plus any LAINF 0.7–1.5% and administrative/cantonal contributions). The Swiss net amount is reduced by about 6-8% due to these withholdings. At the time of the Italian declaration, the taxpayer enters the total amount of withholdings in the EC framework and, thanks to the deductible of €7,500 (if old border) or €10,000 (if new), recovers the tax credit on part of the taxable amount.
In this way, the taxpayer does not suffer double taxation: Switzerland withholds a percentage, Italy recognizes the credit and applies its personal income tax rates only on income that exceeds the deductible. For a family with two children, the additional deductions (universal one-off checks, historically dependant deductions) further reduce the Italian net tax. Coordination with INPS ensures that family allowances are recognised as long as the total income of the family remains within the established limits.
### Difference Between Old Regime and New Agreement Before 1 January 2024, frontier workers were treated with less transparency about deductibles. The New Agreement has standardized the mechanism: a clear line between ### Step-by-step procedure: completing section CE in form 730 1. **Collect documents**: receive from the Swiss employer (or from the competent canton through the municipal tax administration) the certification of source taxes withheld during the year. Also keep December payslips or cantonal tax certificates, as well as any receipts for contributions paid to INPS for pension contributions paid in duplicate. 2. Enter data in section CE: in the Italian 730 form, section "Foreign employment income", enter the gross amount earned in Switzerland (in CHF) and the total amount of source tax withheld, converted to EUR at the exchange rate of the fiscal year-end date. 3. Declare children: in the section "Dependent family members" or "Universal family allowances", list the children with their data (tax ID, date of birth, any personal income). The Revenue Agency will automatically apply deductions if the family income falls within the regulatory limits. 4. Verify the threshold: make sure you have clearly noted whether you are an old cross-border worker (exemption €7,500) or new (threshold €10,000). This determines which portion of income is taxable in Italy and which remains covered by the Swiss tax credit. 5. File the 730: submit the return through a CAF (Tax Assistance Center), a tax advisor, or online on the Revenue Agency portal by the ordinary deadline.
### Deadlines and timelines The deadlines for filing the 730 return follow the standard Italian calendar (generally May-June for the paper form, July for the electronic version). It is advisable to complete the compilation by the ordinary deadline to avoid penalties and quickly receive the tax credit.
### Checklist for cross-border families with children - ☐ Collect source tax certificates from Switzerland (amounts in CHF) - ☐ Verify whether you are old cross-border workers (before 17/7/2023) or new (from 17/7/2023 onwards) - ☐ Convert CHF amounts to EUR (ECB exchange rate at year-end) - ☐ Enter gross amounts and withholdings in section CE of form 730 - ☐ List children and dependent family members with tax ID, date of birth, personal income - ☐ Verify that deductions for children and dependent family members are applied - ☐ Check that the tax credit covers at least the applicable threshold (€7,500 or €10,000)
### Available tools for simulation and further information Use the [cross-border payroll and tax calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate the impact of the threshold, Swiss withholdings (AVS/AI/IPG, LAINF, LPP) and family deductions on your net income. For specific questions about LAMal (health insurance), AVS/AI/LPP pension contributions and coordination with INPS, consult a tax advisor or your local CAF.
Plan your 2026 return with the [cross-border tax calculator](nav:calculator): enter your Swiss gross salary, number of children and family situation, and get an estimate of the tax credit owed. For details on the filing procedure and management of [section CE of form 730](nav:tax-return), we recommend consulting a tax advisor experienced in cross-border matters or the CAF in your canton.

item.title: Border payroll 2026 over 20 km: complete guide
item.description: Swiss paycheck 2026 for border workers over 20 km: withholdings, contributions and real net after the New Agreement in force from 1 January 2024.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Tax at source only in Switzerland for Italian border workers - New Agreement signed on 23/12/2020, effective from 1 January 2024 - Old border guards: exemption €7,500; new: deductible €10,000 - Italy-Switzerland double taxation agreement of 9 December 1976
## Key facts - **What**: Withholding tax withheld exclusively in Switzerland on the income from work of border workers - When: Regime in force from 1 January 2024 (New Agreement signed on 23 December 2020) - Where: Canton of Ticino and the rest of Switzerland; avoidance of double taxation in Italy by means of a tax credit (EC framework of 730) - Who: AFC/ESTV at the federal level and cantonal administrations of contributions for the tax part; INPS for social security - Amount: Old frontier workers exemption €7,500 (transitional regime 2024–2033), new frontier workers exemption €10,000 - When: Italian ratification with Law 83 of 13 June 2023 - Who: SECO, SEM, SUVA among the reference bodies; INPS and Agenzia delle Entrate on the Italian side
From 1 January 2024, the paycheck of the Ticino border worker who works more than 20 km from the border follows completely new tax rules. The New Agreement between Italy and Switzerland, signed in Rome on 23 December 2020 and ratified by Italy with Law 83 of 13 June 2023, redesigned the taxation of frontier workers. Switzerland is not a member of the EU or the EEA: the bilateral relationship is still based on the Convention against Doubles The rates that appear on the paycheck of a Ticino border worker in 2026 are divided into three blocks: social contributions, taxes and insurance. Understanding the difference is essential to reading the slip.
### Swiss social contributions on payroll The AVS/AI/IPG part is equal to 5.3% borne by the employee (out of a total of 10.6% with AVS 2024 reform, half of which is borne by the worker). To this is added the AD (unemployment insurance) contribution of 1.1%, taken up to the ceiling of CHF 148,200. Beyond that threshold, the AC solidarity contribution is triggered, equal to 1% on high incomes. The LAINF premium (accident insurance) varies between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the business risk. The LPP occupational pension, compulsory from the age of 25 for incomes above the coordination threshold, provides for rates between 7% and 18% depending on the age group.
### Italian personal income tax and tax credit For those who are over 20 km from the border and fall under the ordinary regime (not exempt), the Italian personal income tax is applied in three stages: 23% up to €28,000, 35% between €28,001 and €50,000, 43% over €50,000. Double taxation is avoided with the tax credit in the EC framework of model 730: the worker declares foreign income and discharges the tax already paid in Switzerland.
### Scenario comparison: old vs. new border crossers A border crossing already in place before 17 July 2023 enjoys the transitional regime 2024–2033
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). To navigate the 2026 payslip of a cross-border commuter beyond 20 km, it helps to follow a precise path: first identify the deductions, then calculate the real net pay, and finally plan the tax return in Italy.
### 2026 payslip operational checklist 1. Check the deductions on the pay slip. Make sure the following appear: withholding tax (cantonal and communal rate), OASI/DI/IC 5.3%, UI 1.1% (up to CHF 148,200), SUI 1% above the threshold, LAA 0.7–1.5%, LPP 7–18% by age bracket. If any of these items is missing, ask your employer for clarification.
2. Check the allowance or exemption. Old cross-border commuters have an exemption of up to €7,500, new ones up to €10,000. The amount must be compared with the gross annual income converted into euros at the reference exchange rate.
**3. Check LAMal health insurance.** G permit holders can choose between Swiss LAMal (with the right of option) and an equivalent Italian insurance, with standard deductibles between CHF 300 and CHF 2,500 for adults. Do not confuse LAMal with the so-called 'health tax': it is an insurance, not a tax.
4. Keep your pay slips and salary certificate. They are needed for the income tax return in Italy, where the foreign income must be reported in section RC of the 730 form and the foreign tax in section CE as a tax credit.
5. 2026 deadlines. The ordinary deadline for the 730 is the end of September. Repayments are calculated annually; the foreign income tax return is mandatory even when the net Italian tax is zero.

item.title: Opening a bank account in Switzerland: a guide for residents
item.description: Required documents, procedures, management costs and practical advice for border workers working across borders.
item.content:encoded:
## At a glance - A Swiss bank account is essential to receive your salary and operate in the Swiss market - The procedure requires an identity document, proof of residence and employment income certification - Opening times range from 10 to 30 business days depending on the institution - Annual management costs vary according to the account type and services included
## Key facts - **What**: Opening a bank account at a Swiss institution - For whom: Italian residents who work as cross-border commuters in Switzerland - Documents: Valid identification, proof of residence, income documentation - Where: Swiss commercial banks with physical branches or online services - Timing: From 10 to 30 business days from submission of the application - Costs: Variable annual management fees depending on account type - Services: Cross-border transfers, CHF-EUR currency exchange, online banking, recurring payments
### Why a Swiss account is indispensable for the cross-border commuter
Anyone who works as a cross-border commuter beyond the border entrusts a Swiss bank account with the management of their salary in Swiss francs. It is the starting point for operating within the Swiss financial system: salaries are credited here, withholding taxes are deducted, AVS/AI social security contributions are paid, and tax refunds to Italy are handled. Without an account in Switzerland, the cross-border commuter would not be able to receive their salary or have the funds needed for daily expenses on Swiss territory. Choosing the right bank and account type becomes strategic to minimize management costs and access essential services such as cross-border transfers and competitive currency exchange. A [salary calculator](nav:calculator) helps evaluate the impact of Swiss deductions on the actual funds available in the account.
### Who can open an account in Switzerland as an Italian resident
Residency in Italy does not prevent opening an account at a Swiss bank, provided that general identification and documentation requirements are met. Swiss banks have well-established procedures for foreign residents working in Switzerland: they verify identity through a valid identification document, require proof of residential address and, for employees, documentation of the employment relationship (contract, payslip, employer's certificate). Cross-border commuters holding a G Permit benefit from facilitated access at many institutions, thanks to the long-standing relationship between the Swiss banking system and the Italian cross-border commuter population working in Canton Ticino. ### What documents are needed and how the procedure works
Opening an account follows a preliminary identity verification phase (Know Your Customer). The cross-border worker must go to the branch in person with a valid, currently effective identification document: a passport or ID card are the most common. The bank then requires proof of residential address, typically a utility bill, a bank statement, or an official communication in the applicant's name, dated no more than 3-6 months earlier. For employed workers, the third documentary element is the employment contract and a copy of the most recent pay slip, which certify gross income and the employment relationship. Several Swiss banks also request a formal declaration of citizenship and information on the origin of the initial funds (whether first deposit, salary, savings, etc.). It is advisable to contact the chosen institution directly before going to the branch, in order to verify the exact list of documents required and avoid unnecessary visits.
### The main steps of the account opening
The procedure is divided into four main stages. Document collection and form filling: during the branch appointment, the customer fills in the account application form with personal data, residential address, employment information (employer, role, income), and chooses the type of account best suited to their needs. Documentation verification: the bank checks the documents submitted, verifies the data provided, and, if necessary, contacts the employer or the declared residential address directly. This step takes on average 5-15 business days. Decision and outcome: the bank officially communicates whether the application has been accepted. Activation and management: you receive at home the debit card, the PIN, the credentials to access the online portal, and instructions for setting up salary crediting. The overall time from submission of the application to actual use of the account varies between 10 and 30 business days.
### Account types and management costs
Swiss banks offer different categories of accounts, each with different characteristics and pricing. The basic current account is designed for frequent transactions and transfers, with modest annual management costs and low fees on ordinary operations. There are premium accounts that include additional services (securities management, related insurance, access to private advisory services), against higher annual fees. Costs are broken down into a fixed annual fee, commissions on specific transactions (ATM withdrawals, cross-border transfers, CHF-EUR currency exchange), and possible penalties if the account remains inactive for long periods. A cross-border worker who carries out ordinary transactions (salary crediting, bill payments, periodic transfers) should not encounter hidden costs, provided they choose a basic account suited to their needs. Compare offers from at least two institutions before deciding. The differences in [cost of living](nav:cost-of-living) between Switzerland and Italy require careful management of the banking component as well.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### How to start the account opening process: step-by-step procedure
Step 1: Identify the most suitable bank. Evaluate which banking institution best meets your needs by considering: location of the branch closest to your workplace, services offered (online banking, mobile app, customer service toll-free number), stated management costs, and availability of cross-border services (transfers to Italy, CHF-EUR exchange at competitive rates, services for cross-border commuters).
Step 2: Gather and verify the documentation. Collect a valid identity document (passport or ID card with a future expiry date), recent proof of residence (utility bill no older than 6 months, official communication with address), the original employment contract or a certified copy, and payslips from the last 1-3 months. If available, also prepare a letter from your employer certifying your employment position. Contact the bank in advance to ask if any additional documentation is required.
Step 3: Contact the institution and set up an appointment. Access the bank's website or call the nearest branch to book a meeting with a bank employee. Many Swiss institutions also offer video interviews for new clients, reducing the need to physically go to the branch during the very first steps.
Step 4: Submit the application and fill out the forms. During the appointment (at the branch or via video), complete the account opening form providing full personal details, your residential address in Italy, employment details, gross income, and preferences regarding the type of account. Submit the original documentation (the employee will check that everything is in order).
Step 5: Wait for the internal verification. The bank processes the request, verifies the data provided, performs compliance checks, and if necessary contacts the employer or the declared residential address for confirmation. This step typically takes 5-15 business days.
Step 6: Outcome communication and activation. You will receive an official letter or email confirming the account opening. The debit card will then be sent to your home (usually within 1-2 weeks), the PIN via secure mail, and the login credentials for the bank's online portal.
### Final details and next steps
Once you have received the card and the PIN, access the bank's online portal and activate the main services: set up your salary payment with your employer by providing the Swiss IBAN and account number, configure transaction alerts via SMS or email, and familiarise yourself with the platform for transfers, recurring payments (rent, utilities), and consulting account statements. If possible, make a first test payment to ensure everything works. Remember that as a cross-border commuter you will face tax issues related to Swiss income: taxable amounts are subject to withholding tax in Switzerland, and you will need to include the income in your Italian tax return to avoid double taxation (the tax credit in section CE of the 730 form covers the Swiss tax). For clarification on tax and contribution obligations towards INPS, contact a tax consultant specialising in cross-border law or contact the Revenue Agency directly. The [cross-border bank accounts](nav:banks) on the site offer comparisons between the main options available for those who work in Switzerland.
Evaluating a Ticino job offer? Simulate your [net payslip](nav:payslip): enter gross salary, marital status and municipality for a detailed breakdown.

item.title: Remote Work While on Vacation: Taxation and Rights of Cross-Border Workers
item.description: When the border worker works remotely from a third country during the holidays: what changes for taxes, LAMal and AVS. Everything you need to communicate to the employer.
item.content:encoded:
## At a Glance - Withholding tax in Switzerland: Nothing changes if you work remotely from abroad - The new Cross-Border Workers Agreement, effective January 1, 2024, does not introduce any specific prohibitions - LAMal and AVS coverage continue as usual even while working remotely from abroad - Notify your employer before your vacation regarding contractual and insurance matters
## Key Facts - **What**: Remote work by cross-border workers from a third country during vacation - When: New regulations effective January 1, 2024 - Where: Third country (outside Italy, typically within the EU or beyond) - Who: Cross-border workers with a G permit (employees) - Tax: Withholding tax remains in Switzerland; tax return filed in Italy with an EU tax credit - Coverage: LAMal remains mandatory and valid with an EHIC in the EU - Notification: Mandatory to the employer before the remote work vacation
### The tax regime remains unchanged
A cross-border worker with a G permit who works remotely from a foreign beach during vacation is in a situation that requires contractual clarity but does not entail any tax surprises. The good news: withholding tax continues to be collected exclusively in Switzerland. No two countries tax you at the same time—this is how the system has worked for cross-border workers since the signing of the Italian-Swiss Convention on December 9, 1976.
Italy recognizes the tax credit in Section CE of Form 730: this means that the amount already paid as Swiss withholding tax reduces your Italian taxable income, thereby preventing double taxation. If you are an existing cross-border worker (already registered before July 17, 2023), you are entitled to an annual exemption of €7,500 under the transitional regime (2024–2033); if you are a new cross-border worker, the exemption is €10,000. In both cases, remote work from a third country does not affect this benefit.
The New Cross-Border Workers Agreement, signed on December 23, 2020, and effective as of January 1, 2024 (Italian Law No. 83 of June 13, 2023), reaffirms the regulatory framework and introduces rules on withholdings and tax transitions, but does not add specific prohibitions on remote work from abroad. This means that even new cross-border workers need not fear any surprises: the single Swiss withholding tax remains the standard mechanism.
### Mandatory Contributions: AVS, LPP, Insurance
AVS/AI/IPG contributions continue to be paid regularly (5.3% paid by the employee); accident insurance (AD/AC, 1.1% on salary up to CHF 148,200) and the LAINF contribution (0.7–1.5%) remain in effect. The LPP (occupational pension plan, 7–18% depending on age group starting at age 25) continues to accrue without interruption. Whether you’re working from Barcelona or a terrace in Portugal makes no difference: your Swiss pay stub tracks everything as if you had never left your desk at the office.
The LAMal (mandatory health insurance) remains valid during your remote work period. Cross-border workers with a G permit have the right to choose between Swiss LAMal coverage (private, with annual deductibles for adults ranging from CHF 300 to 2,500) or maintaining Italian coverage under the CMI agreement. In either case, coverage remains in effect. If you are in an EU country, the EHIC (European Health Insurance Card) guarantees access to public health services; if you travel outside the EU, contact your insurer to verify whether your coverage extends geographically.
### Notification to the Employer: A Critical Issue
The real issue is not a tax matter, but rather a contractual and insurance matter. The employer must be aware that the cross-border employee is working remotely from abroad. Not because the New Agreement requires it, but because: - Some employment contracts limit remote work to Swiss or EU territory only - The employer’s general liability insurance, SUVA (if applicable), and accident insurance policies may have geographic exclusions - The employer has the right to verify connection stability, availability, and performance
Communicating in writing (via email to your direct supervisor) is the proper procedure: “I will be on a remote vacation from [start date] to [end date] in [Country]. I will remain available and reachable via [phone number/email]. I confirm that I will access company systems remotely via VPN.” This clarifies the situation, avoids misunderstandings, and protects both parties. ### Three Real-World Scenarios: How It Works in Practice
Scenario 1: Long-term Cross-Border Worker with a €7,500 Exemption
A cross-border worker registered as such before July 17, 2023, is entitled to an annual €7,500 exemption (transitional regime 2024–2033). Their gross monthly pay is CHF 5,500 (approximately €5,300). Swiss withholding tax applies at both the federal and cantonal levels (average rates in Ticino: ~10% federal, plus the cantonal rate). During two weeks of remote work from Valencia, withholding tax continues to be deducted from his paycheck as usual: no interruption, no exception. Upon returning from vacation, he reports the income on the Italian 730 tax return: Italian tax (IRPEF rate of 23% up to €28,000, 35% from €28,001 to €50,000, 43% above €50,000) applies to the portion not already taxed by Switzerland thanks to the tax credit (Section CE). The benefit of the €7,500 exemption remains intact: it is a structural benefit, not tied to the physical location of employment.
Scenario 2: New Cross-Border Worker with a €10,000 Exemption
A cross-border worker who entered the system after July 17, 2023, benefits from an annual exemption of €10,000: €2,500 more than existing cross-border workers. The logic is the same: a single tax in Switzerland, a tax credit in Italy, and no double taxation. Two weeks of remote work from a resort in Croatia does not negate the benefit. The tax-free allowance continues to apply over 12 months; the remote work period is normally included in the annual calculation.
Scenario 3: LAMal During a Remote Work Vacation Abroad
The cross-border worker has Swiss LAMal coverage (CSS, Helsana, Assura, or similar). They are away for 10 days in Portugal and continue to work part-time from their laptop. The LAMal remains active and provides coverage even abroad, thanks to the EHIC card (valid in the EU/EEA). If an accident occurs—a fall, gastroenteritis, or a bruise—the coverage applies: simply present the EHIC card or document at the Portuguese emergency room. Expenses are covered (with any deductibles as specified in the LAMal contract). There is no suspension, and no extra fees for “working from abroad.” Upon returning to Switzerland, everything is in order. The Swiss LAMal makes no distinction between office work and remote work from the beach: it covers the insured person, wherever they are.
### Double Taxation: How the Mechanism Works
The Italian-Swiss Agreement of December 9, 1976, established that cross-border workers pay taxes in the Swiss canton where they work. Italy recognizes this through a **tax credit**, entered in Section CE of the 730 tax return: it’s a line that reads “tax already paid in Switzerland = CHF X, converted to EUR: Y, recognized as a credit.” The result is that Italian taxation applies only to the “residual portion” of income—that is, the portion not yet taxed by Switzerland. No double taxation.
The New Cross-Border Workers Agreement (2024) does not change this logic; rather, it further solidifies it with new exemptions (for existing cross-border workers) and tax-free allowances (for new ones). Working from Spain, Portugal, or France for 1–2 weeks does not alter this mechanism: the Swiss withholding tax remains the sole tax, and Italy applies the tax credit.
### Insurance Aspects: SUVA, Liability Insurance, Data Protection
If the cross-border worker is employed at a company location in Switzerland, SUVA (Swiss National Accident Insurance Institute) covers any accidents. If they work remotely from abroad, SUVA coverage remains tied to the employment contract: some employers extend coverage wherever the employee works (“work anywhere”), while others limit it to Switzerland or the EU. Discussing this with the employer clarifies the matter.
Corporate liability insurance (if the cross-border worker uses company equipment or handles sensitive data) may also have geographic exclusions. For example: “Coverage valid for employees working within Swiss territory”—in which case, teleworking from Morocco might not be covered. Checking the contract and informing your employer reduces this risk.
Finally, data protection: working on a public Wi-Fi network at a foreign hotel exposes you to cyber risks (data breaches, stolen credentials). The best practice is to use a VPN (virtual private network) provided by your employer, so that traffic is encrypted and your credentials are not transmitted in plain text. This is basic security common sense, not a tax requirement, but it is part of being transparent with your employer. ### Practical Checklist: Before, During, and After a Remote Vacation
**One Week Before**
1. Send an email to your employer (immediate supervisor or HR): "I would like to work remotely from [Country] from [start date] to [end date]. I’ll remain operational and available via [phone number/email]. I confirm that I have remote access to company systems via VPN. Can you confirm that this is permitted under my employment contract?”
2. Review your employment contract: Does the section on “place of work” or “telework” specify whether international remote work is permitted? If the contract states “Switzerland only” or “EU only,” teleworking from a non-EU country could violate the terms of your contract.
3. Check your LAMal/CMI coverage: If you’re traveling to the EU, bring your EHIC (European Health Insurance Card). If you’re traveling outside the EU (Morocco, Turkey, Egypt, USA), call your insurer: “Will I remain covered if I work remotely in [Country] for 2 weeks?”
4. Backups and security: Back up your important local files. Download a reliable VPN (some employers provide one) before you leave. Do not use unsecured public Wi-Fi at hotels.
During your remote vacation
- Access company systems only via VPN, never directly over public Wi-Fi - Stick to office hours: if you’re in the UTC+2 time zone (Portugal during summer) and the office is in UTC+1 (Ticino during summer), be available at least in the morning for synchronous meetings - Track your work hours (timesheet, if required by the company) - Keep receipts for extra expenses (additional internet connection, coworking space if needed)—they may be deductible as business expenses, even though working from home abroad generally does not qualify for tax breaks in Italy - Stay reachable: check email at least twice a day, and respond within 4–6 hours
Upon Return
- No administrative formalities: the New Cross-Border Workers Agreement does not require notifications to SECO (Swiss State Secretariat for Economic Affairs) or SEM (Swiss State Secretariat for Migration) for short periods of remote work abroad - Your paycheck remains the same - The Italian 730 tax return includes the income as if it had never left Switzerland: Section CE applies the tax credit against the Swiss withholding tax - No “accruals” or “allocations”: taxation is continuous, regardless of where you were physically located
### When You Don’t Need to Report Anything
If the vacation is purely personal (no work): - 2 weeks at the beach, no emails, no laptop, no meetings - Standard vacation: your employer already knows you won’t be available - No special reporting required, no tax implications regarding remote work
But if you turn on your laptop even for a single teleconference, then it’s a “remote vacation”: you must report it. The line is fine but important for transparency.
### Internal Resources and Tools
To better understand the tax implications of your remote vacation, it’s helpful to simulate the net pay calculation:
- [Calcolatore stipendio frontaliere](nav:calculator): Simulate a pay stub with Swiss withholdings, AVS/LPP contributions, and bonuses to understand the net amount after federal and cantonal taxes - [Guida LAMal per frontalieri](nav:health): Explore Swiss health coverage options, deductibles, and coverage abroad with the EHIC - [Ristorni e dichiarazione 730](nav:tax-return): Calculate your Italian tax refund and verify how the CE section applies the tax credit from Switzerland
### Conclusion: Transparency = No Surprises
Working remotely from a third country while on vacation does not exempt you from Swiss tax obligations—withholding tax continues as usual—nor does it exclude you from LAMal and AVS coverage—which remain valid and in effect. What changes is your physical location: Notifying your employer of your remote work abroad is an act of contractual and insurance transparency, not an additional regulatory requirement.
The New Cross-Border Workers Agreement (effective January 1, 2024) maintains the single taxation regime in Switzerland and the Italian tax credit, without adding complexity for short-term remote work abroad. Whether you’re an “old” cross-border worker (€7,500 exemption) or a “new” one (€10,000 exemption), teleworking from Spain, Portugal, or France doesn’t affect your benefit: it continues to apply over a 12-month period, regardless of where you physically work.
When you return and receive your next paycheck: it will be identical to before. When you file your 730 tax return in April: your foreign income from the vacation period is treated as Swiss income, and the tax credit reduces your Italian taxable income. One tax, no double taxation, no surprises.

item.title: Remote from holiday abroad: tax guide for border workers
item.description: Working remotely while on holiday abroad does not change Swiss taxes and LAMal coverage remains active. Here's what you need to check and communicate to the employer.
item.content:encoded:
## In a nutshell - Tax at source: withheld in Switzerland, not in the holiday country - LAMal: coverage guaranteed everywhere, but check with the insurer - Communicate to the employer: recommended administrative practice before departure
## Key facts - **What**: Continue working remotely during a holiday in a third country - When: Temporary period of stay abroad (days or weeks) - Where: Any country outside Switzerland (EU, EEA, non-EU) - Who: Border with G Permit and Swiss contract - Legal basis: Italian-Swiss Convention of 9 December 1976
A border worker who continues to work remotely while on holiday abroad does not incur double taxation. The income tax at source is withheld exclusively from Switzerland, as established by the Italian-Swiss Convention of 9 December 1976. This principle remains valid regardless of where the border worker is physically at the time of execution of the work.
However, the situation is complex because it touches on the issue of temporary residence. During the holiday period, the border worker maintains his/her ordinary residence and personal registration, while the stay abroad is exceptional. Italy avoids double taxation on income from employment through the tax credit (EC framework of the annual tax return, Form 730). Therefore, any tax due in Italy is calculated net of tax ### Taxation and tax at source: what changes and what doesn't
Taxation on income from employment for a border worker follows the principle of the place of performance of the benefit. Since the frontier worker is formally employed at a Swiss company, the Swiss source tax is the correct tax, regardless of where the work is physically performed at that time. This is particularly relevant during a holiday: the fact that the border worker temporarily stays in a third country (France, Spain, Austria, Greece, Portugal) DOES NOT trigger a parallel taxation in the holiday country for that income. European laws generally do not tax income from services performed remotely to a Swiss employer.
Swiss rates remain unchanged: withholding tax withholding continues according to federal and cantonal tables. Employee social contributions (AVS/AI/IPG at 5.3%, AD/AC at 1.1% up to CHF 148,200 of wage bill, LAINF between 0.7% and 1.5%, LPP between 7% and 18% depending on the age group from 25 years onwards) remain ordinary. None of these amounts change according to the place of performance of the service.
Compulsory LAMal insurance guarantees 24-hour coverage, even in the event of a medical emergency in the holiday country. Emergency benefits are covered by the Swiss health insurance fund by virtue of the domiciliation in the LAMal registers, even if temporarily absent
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### What to Communicate to Your Employer Before a Working Vacation
The first step is to inform the HR manager and your direct supervisor that you will be working remotely from a foreign location. Although there is no explicit legal obligation to do so, it is a common administrative practice and prevents misunderstandings regarding availability, time zones, and compliance with company remote work policies. Many Swiss companies already have procedures in place for remote work; informing your employer of the duration of your stay abroad allows for transparent coordination and demonstrates professional responsibility.
Aspects to report to your employer: - Precise period of the working vacation (from… to…) - Country of stay and time zone difference - Confirmation of your availability for meetings and critical deadlines - Verification that the remote Internet connection is stable and secure (VPN, privacy, compliance with company cybersecurity protocols)
### Checks with LAMal Insurance and Banks
Before leaving, contact your Swiss health insurance fund to clarify whether coverage includes emergency care in your destination country, what documents or procedures are necessary in case of a medical visit, and whether prior authorization is required for planned treatments. LAMal usually covers emergencies, but reimbursement timelines and procedures vary.
Also contact your bank to inform them of the situation, so that recurring payments (mortgage, insurance, utilities) are not disrupted due to a temporary address change or atypical transactions from your vacation area.
### Documentation and Record-Keeping
Keep a copy of your travel documentation (hotel booking, tickets) and a self-certification of your working vacation period. Although the Italian Revenue Agency (Agenzia delle Entrate) and the Swiss Federal Customs Administration (AFC/ESTV) do not systematically check this during a short stay, organized documentation is useful in case a future tax issue arises. Also keep a record of the actual working dates during your vacation, in case your employer requires certification.
For an accurate estimate of your net pay during remote work and contributions paid, [consult our net calculator](nav:calculator). If you wish to explore the specific tax issues of your cross-border worker situation, discover the [refunds tool](nav:ristorni) and check your [Permit G](nav:permits) status and its implications.

## In a nutshell - Azzio is in Varese, near the Ticino border for cross-border commuting - Permit G allows you to work in Ticino with Italian residence - New agreement 2024: €10,000 deductible for new frontier workers, €7,500 exemption for historians
## Key facts - **What**: Italian residence with work in Ticino (G permit) - When: Effective date of new border agreement from 1 January 2024 - Where: Azzio (Varese) – Ticino-Italy border - Who: Frontier workers G - Excess amount: €10,000 new, €7,500 old border guards (transitional regime 2024–2033)
Living in Azzio and working in Ticino is a choice that affects thousands of border workers. The geographical location of the municipality in the province of Varese, close to the Ticino border, and the cost of living in Italy make this scenario attractive compared to direct residence in Switzerland. However, those who decide to move must be aware of the new border agreement that entered into force on 1 January 2024, which significantly modifies the taxation of employee income in Switzerland.
The agreement, signed on 23 December 2020 and ratified by Italy with Law 83 of 13 June 2023, introduces a deductible of €10,000 for new border workers and a transitional partial exemption regime for those who are already border workers (€7,500 from 2024 to 2033). These news directly affect the net paycheck and the Italian tax return. It is therefore not possible ### How taxation works for the border crossing from Azzio
Taxation on employee income in Switzerland is covered by the tax at source, a withholding made only in Switzerland by the employer. Italy does not apply parallel withholding taxes to border workers, thanks to the Italian-Swiss Convention signed on 9 December 1976. This means that there is no 'double taxation': income is taxed only once by Switzerland.
The effective rate varies depending on the income bracket, cantonal and federal. Switzerland withholds these amounts directly in the paycheck. Italy recognises a tax credit in form 730 (EC framework) to offset taxes already paid in Switzerland. Those with a modest income from employment in Ticino can get significant refunds thanks to this mechanism.
### The new 2024 agreement: refreshments and deductibles
The new border agreement that entered into force on 1 January 2024 modifies the calculation of the tax at source. New frontier workers (those who started working after 17 July 2023) benefit from a deductible of €10,000 per year on which the tax is not calculated. Those who were already border workers enter a transitional regime with an exemption of €7,500 from 2024 to 2033. This means a reduction in direct payroll withholding compared to the previous regime.
### Swiss contributions: AVS, LPP and LAMal
Those who work in Ticino pay the AVS (basic pension) at 5.3% of the salary
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Pre-transfer Checklist for Azzio
Anyone deciding to relocate to Azzio to work in Ticino must follow certain administrative steps. First and foremost, it is necessary to find and sign an employment contract with a Ticino employer before proceeding: the G permit is conditional on a job offer. In parallel, you must:
1. Reserve a residence in Azzio (rental or owned property) with documentation (rental contract or deed). 2. Submit your G permit application to the SEM (State Secretariat for Migration) of the Canton of Ticino. 3. Register at the Italian registry office in Azzio (enrollment in the Population Register). 4. Enroll in Swiss social insurance (AVS/AI/LPP) through your employer. 5. Subscribe to health insurance (LAMal in Switzerland or remain in the Italian health system, your choice). 6. Inform the Italian Revenue Agency of your change of residence and your status as a cross-border worker.
Some of these operations can happen in parallel; others must precede the actual transfer. The G permit is generally not granted until your residence in Italy is actually established.
### Timelines and Deadlines
The actual transfer to Azzio is a process that typically requires 4-6 weeks from signing the employment contract to receiving the permit and completing the registry registration. However, timelines vary depending on the speed of the Italian local authorities and Swiss cantonal services.
Once you have relocated, cross-border workers must file their Italian tax return every year by May 31 (ordinary deadline for form 730) or June 30 (Unico form). This deadline is crucial for obtaining tax refunds and to inform the Italian Revenue Agency of your status as a resident of Azzio working in Switzerland. Failure to meet this deadline means you cannot recover the tax credit in subsequent years.
### Tools and Support
To estimate your net salary after Swiss withholding tax, AVS/LPP contributions, and the exemption from the new agreement, use the [calculator](nav:calculator) from Frontaliere Ticino. If you have been working in Ticino for more than one year and have not yet claimed tax refunds, consult the [refunds guide](nav:ristorni) to understand how to calculate and declare them to the Italian tax authorities.
To learn more about the details of the G permit and the differences with the B permit (residence in Switzerland), access the [permit comparator](nav:permit-compare). If you have specific pension planning needs, our [pension calculator](nav:pension) helps you quantify your second and third pillar benefits in relation to the cross-border worker regime.
Relocating from an Italian municipality to the Ticino border is an important decision: take time to evaluate the cost of living, commuting times, and tax implications for your specific situation. Make use of our tools and stay updated on cross-border regulations that change with each new agreement.

Lomazzo is a municipality in the province of Como, in Lombardy, located a few kilometres from the main border crossings with Ticino. The proximity to Brogeda, Chiasso and Ponte Tresa makes the transfer from Lomazzo a practical choice for border workers who wish to combine a lower cost of living than Ticino with access to the Swiss labour market.
The tax regime for border workers is governed by the Convention between Italy and Switzerland (9 December 1976) and the New Frontier Agreement, which entered into force on 1 January 2024 following Italian ratification with Law 83 ### Cost of living: the economic advantage of Lomazzo
The cost-of-living differential between Lomazzo and Ticino is the first concrete incentive to move. While Ticino offers competitive salaries aligned with the Swiss market, the cost of housing, services and daily spending in Lomazzo remains significantly lower.
The properties in Lomazzo (sales, rentals, utilities) are priced according to the Italian and continental European market, not according to the Swiss market. This allows the border worker to save a substantial fraction of the Swiss gross income compared to those residing in Ticino. Access to shops, medical, school and recreational services follows Italian prices.
### Tax and contribution aspects for the border crossing
A border worker who resides in Lomazzo and works in Ticino is subject to:
**Tax at source in Switzerland**: it is ONLY withheld in Switzerland on income from work. The Italy-Switzerland Convention (9 December 1976) and the New Agreement avoid double taxation. Italy recognizes the tax credit (EC framework of declaration 730) for foreign income, guaranteeing the border worker not to pay twice on the same income.
Swiss social contributions (AVS/AI/IPG): 5.3% borne by the employee, paid directly from employment in Ticino.

Travel times vary significantly depending on the season, road incidents at the border crossings, and Alpine weather conditions.
#### Housing and residential context
Visit Lomazzo at different times of the year to check the residential environment, school services (if relevant for your household), medical services, shops, and leisure options. Consult local real estate agents to understand the rental and purchase market. Also check the availability and quality of local public transport (buses, trains).
#### Contract and job stability
Make sure your employment contract in Ticino is stable (preferably permanent) before committing to an international move. The G permit is tied to employment; losing your job leads to a review of your residence authorization.
#### Preliminary consultations and paperwork
Before the move: 1. Consult an accountant or tax advisor specialized in Italy-Switzerland cross-border commuters to align your Italian 730 tax return, Ticino cantonal taxes, and AVS contributions. 2. Verify your insurance coverage: LAMal (choice between Swiss or Italian INPS), car liability, home policies. 3. Open a bank account in Switzerland if you do not already have one (useful for receiving salaries and making local payments). 4. Register with the Italian registry office in Lomazzo and notify the Italian Revenue Agency (Agenzia delle Entrate) of your change of residence.
#### Practical tools and resources
To calculate the net tax impact of moving from Lomazzo to Ticino, use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) from Frontaliere Ticino: enter the Swiss gross salary, the Ticino cantonal and municipal tax rates, and you will get a realistic monthly/annual net estimate.

Living in Lomazzo and working in Ticino is an economically convenient choice thanks to the cost-of-living differential and the tax incentives for cross-border commuters (€10,000 allowance from 2024 onwards). The geographical proximity to the Brogeda and Chiasso border crossings, combined with careful planning of documents, permits, taxes, and contract, makes Lomazzo a solid base for those who want to balance Swiss income with the cost of living in the Italian border area.

## Key facts - **What**: G Permit Frontier, Schignano-Ticino - When: From 1 January 2024 (New Agreement in force) - Where: Lombardy → Canton Ticino - Who: Employee, INPS + AVS - Tax: Withholding only in CH; IT personal income tax 23-43% (with credit for CH taxes) - CH contributions: AVS/AI/IPG 5.3%, LPP 7-18%, LAINF 0.7-1.5% - Permit: G (border), 5 years renewable
The border worker who lives in Schignano, Lombardy, and works in Ticino falls under the regime of cross-border workers regulated by the Italian-Swiss Convention of 9 December 1976 and the New Frontier Agreement (signed on 23 December 2020, in force from 1 January 2024). This status has tax, social security and organisational implications that differ significantly from the pure Italian employee or Swiss resident.
### Taxation of the Schignano-Ticino border crossing
Income tax at source is only withheld in Switzerland. The frontier worker does not pay double taxation: Italy avoids the double burden by resorting to the tax credit in the EC Framework form of the tax return (730). ### Social security contributions and compulsory insurance
The border crossing paid in Ticino adheres to the Swiss social security system. The AVS (old-age disability pension), AI (disability insurance) and IPG (loss of earnings allowance) are retained to the extent of 5.3% on the gross salary for the employee; the company pays the additional 5.3% on behalf of the worker. In addition there are unemployment insurance contributions (AD/AC) of 1.1%, limited to a ceiling of CHF 148,200 per annum, and accident insurance (LAINF) between 0.7 and 1.5%. To these is added occupational pension insurance (LPP), the second Swiss pillar, which represents a share between 7 and 18% of the gross salary depending on the age group (from 25 years). While AVS/AI/IPG are mandatory by law, the LPP is conditional on registration with the company's pension fund.
At the same time, the border worker remains registered with the Italian INPS for the payment of Italian social security contributions (about 9-10% of the declared income), with which he accumulates pension rights in the Italian system. This double contribution is lawful and does not generate conflict: each country recognizes the contribution paid in the other in the event of progress towards retirement.

The administrative path involves three main steps. **First: G Permit application.** The cantonal Migration offices (SEM) or the cantonal police authority where the work will take place (Ticino) must be contacted. The application must be submitted jointly by the Swiss employer and the future employee. Required documents include: a valid passport or ID card, certificate of good conduct, employment contract, and documentation of the employer's registration with the Companies Register. The G Permit has long-term validity (generally 5 years, renewable) and allows daily commuting from the place of residence in Italy to the workplace in Ticino.
Second: simultaneous INPS registration. Once employed in Ticino, the worker must register with the Italian INPS as a salaried employee, reporting the expected gross Swiss income and the job category. This creates the Italian social security file alongside the Swiss AVS. The Swiss employer usually assists in transmitting social security data to the Italian authorities (CE coordination forms). Third: LAMal choice. Within the deadlines set by the employer (usually 3 months from hiring), the cross-border commuter declares whether to remain covered by the Italian CMI or to opt for a Swiss LAMal. The choice is not binding in perpetuity, but changing coverage requires notification to the employer and the relevant funds.

Before the transition from Schignano, it is advisable to check: the location of the workplace in Ticino (Chiasso, Mendrisio, Lugano, Bellinzona, Locarno), which determines the withholding tax rate and the competent canton for the permit; nationality and passport (the G Permit is issued to EU/EFTA citizens, with a simplified procedure); the Italian contribution history, to avoid gaps in INPS registration.
